body.rationale:
Equal weight is the only method in the roster that makes no estimate at all, so it carries no estimation error from the CMAs or from the covariance matrix. DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal (2009) found that optimised portfolios rarely beat 1/N out of sample, because estimation error swamps the gain from optimising. Here that argument is concrete. The CMAs are judged, blended forecasts, and a method that consumes them inherits their errors. Maximum Sharpe, Black-Litterman and the resampled frontier all concentrate on small differences between those forecasts.

The ex-ante numbers are respectable, not exceptional. Expected return is 6.84% at 8.41% volatility, Sharpe 0.36, with 18.0 effective assets out of 18, so there is no concentration risk. The portfolio is compliant with the draft IPS, which is unusual: the free-run results show that most risk-based methods pile into cash at 0.6-2.5% volatility and fall below the 8% floor. Equal weight reaches the band without any parameter tuning, so nothing about this proposal is an artefact of pushing a method toward the band. It is simply what a no-information prior produces.

The regime supports the case only modestly. In an expansion, risk assets are rewarded, and the large equity, credit, REIT and commodity sleeves add return that a covariance-driven method would shun. The covariance-based methods did well in the late-cycle regime the paper studied (§4.3), but that is not the regime here, so the argument for deferring to the covariance structure is weaker. Equal weight also serves the CIO as a neutral anchor. An ensemble that tilts away from it should be able to say what information justifies the tilt.

The tracking error against the IPS benchmark is 4.36%. That is a real active bet: the benchmark holds a large US large-cap and intermediate-Treasury core, and equal weight underweights both, and holds more of every other asset, by default. It is not a view, just a consequence of ignoring the benchmark's shape. I flag it so reviewers do not mistake it for conviction.
body.notes: Key assumption: Expected returns, volatilities and correlations are too noisy to estimate reliably for this 18-asset universe, so any use of them adds more estimation error than the information it captures, and a naive prior beats an optimised guess. Main weakness: It ignores risk entirely. Each asset gets the same capital whatever its volatility, so risk contributions are very unequal: equities, REITs, commodities, high yield and EM debt dominate portfolio variance, while cash and short Treasuries get the same capital but add almost no risk or return, which is a drag. About 5.6% of capital sits in cash, plus more in short-duration bonds, that a return-aware method would deploy. It also takes a 4.36% tracking-error bet against the benchmark through its construction, not by choice. Its compliance with the IPS is also a coincidence of the asset mix, not something the method aims at, so a change in volatilities could move it out of the band without any change in the method. Preferred when: When forecast quality is low or the CMAs disagree with the market-implied returns, when the covariance estimate is unstable or short-history assets make it unreliable, and in a risk-on expansion where holding many risk assets is rewarded. It is also preferred as the benchmark that any more complex method must beat, and as the ensemble anchor when the CIO wants to limit model risk and the combined portfolio must stay inside the IPS band. Invalidated if: It is the wrong choice if the CMAs prove reliable enough to beat the naive prior: if return differences across asset classes are large and persistent, a method that uses them should win. It is also wrong if the regime turns toward a drawdown or late-cycle stress in which equities, credit and commodities fall together, because equal weight is heavily exposed to those correlated risk sleeves. A volatility rise that takes the portfolio outside the 8-12% band, or a draft IPS revision that adds per-asset caps, benchmark-relative limits or tighter tracking-error limits, would also weaken it. Finally, if the covariance matrix is well estimated and stable, risk-based methods such as risk parity or maximum diversification would dominate it on risk-adjusted terms.
